I'm not exactly sure if it was a whole month. It's hard to keep track of time like that, you know? Time just sort of blends together, especially when you're working flat rate at the shop. You're just trying to beat the book time on every job so you can actually make a decent paycheck. The whole steering column, the airbags, the center console—everything has to come out just to get to this one little plastic box against the firewall. 

I actually had a customer yell at me once because his car was in the shop for three days for a heater core. He kept saying, "It's just a little radiator, how hard can it be?" People have no idea. They think cars are still built like they were in the seventies, where you could actually fit your hand between the engine block and the radiator fan. Now everything is packed in so tight you need specialized, low-profile ratchets just to change a spark plug. I spent a hundred and fifty bucks off the tool truck last week just for this one flex-head wrench. The tool truck guys are basically loan sharks, I swear. They pull up every Tuesday, hand you a complimentary donut, and suddenly you're in debt for the next five years because you just had to have the new impact gun with the fancy green casing...

But yeah, I don't know if the quiet period lasted a full month. It was just a while.

They had the best salsa verde, it was so spicy it would make your ears ring, but you couldn't stop eating it. I tried making it at home once, but I couldn't get the tomatillos to roast right. They just got mushy and stuck to the pan...\n\nWait, sorry. Yes. Even when my energy was totally normal and I was sleeping fine, the voice and the tracking stuff never stopped.\n\nDoctor: Did the voice first start soon after you had any serious medical problem, head injury, or seizure?\n\nPatient: No, nothing like that. I haven't had any seizures or big medical issues. I mean, I bump my head on the lift arms at the shop sometimes, but just normal bumps. Those lift arms are solid steel, though. You learn pretty quick to wear a bump cap if you're working under a low clearance. We had this one guy, Gary, who refused to wear one, and he stood right up into the oil drain plug of an F-250. Cut his scalp wide open. Scalp wounds bleed like crazy, you know? It looked like a horror movie in bay three. We had to use like three bags of that industrial absorbent floor sweep just to clean it up. \n\nThat floor sweep is basically just glorified kitty litter, honestly. I don't know why the shop suppliers charge so much for it. I buy the cheap stuff for my cat, Barnaby, but he kicks it absolutely everywhere. I had to get him one of those enclosed boxes with the little plastic flap door, but he just sits in there and bats the door back and forth for hours. It makes this clicking sound that drives me crazy when I'm trying to watch TV. He's a good cat, though. Found him behind a dumpster at the tire shop. He was just a tiny little thing, covered in grease...\n\nUm, wait. Head injuries? Right. No, no serious head injuries or anything for me. I've always been pretty healthy.\n\nDoctor: During that time when your sleep and energy felt normal, did the voice continue for at least one full month?\n\nPatient: I'm not exactly sure if it was a whole month. It's hard to keep track of time like that, you know? Time just sort of blends together, especially when you're working flat rate at the shop. You're just trying to beat the book time on every job so you can actually make a decent paycheck. Like, the book might say replacing a heater core takes eight hours, which is a joke because on some of these newer SUVs, you have to pull the entire dashboard out. The whole steering column, the airbags, the center console—everything has to come out just to get to this one little plastic box against the firewall. \n\nI actually had a customer yell at me once because his car was in the shop for three days for a heater core. He kept saying, \"It's just a little radiator, how hard can it be?\" People have no idea. They think cars are still built like they were in the seventies, where you could actually fit your hand between the engine block and the radiator fan. Now everything is packed in so tight you need specialized, low-profile ratchets just to change a spark plug. I spent a hundred and fifty bucks off the tool truck last week just for this one flex-head wrench. The tool truck guys are basically loan sharks, I swear. They pull up every Tuesday, hand you a complimentary donut, and suddenly you're in debt for the next five years because you just had to have the new impact gun with the fancy green casing...\n\nBut yeah, I don't know if the quiet period lasted a full month. It was just a while.\n\nDoctor: At any point, did the voice continue for a full month while your mood and energy felt normal?\n\nPatient: Well, like I said, it was definitely a few weeks. It was a quieter time, you know? I was actually sleeping a lot more, and I wasn't staying up making all those huge plans for my custom shop. I felt pretty normal, energy-wise. But even then, I still heard the voice out in the garage, and I still knew for a fact that my husband and my boss were tracking me. \n\nSpeaking of my boss, he actually brought in donuts the other day. Glazed ones from that place over on 4th Street. They’re good, but they always leave that sticky glaze all over your fingers, which is the last thing you want when you’re about to grab a torque wrench. If your hands are sticky, all the grease and brake dust just clings to you. I usually use this heavy-duty pumice soap we have in the washroom, the kind that feels like you're scrubbing your hands with actual sand. It takes off everything, even that black RTV silicone sealant. That silicone is a nightmare if you get it on your clothes. I ruined a perfectly good pair of Dickies work pants last month because I brushed up against a water pump I had just sealed. The pants were practically new, too. I had just bought them because my old ones were getting holes in the knees from kneeling on the concrete all day. You'd think they'd make a decent knee pad for mechanics, but the ones they sell always slide down around your ankles the second you start walking. I saw this guy on YouTube who actually cut up an old yoga mat and glued it inside his pants... \n\nWait, what were you asking? Oh, right. Yeah, even during those quieter weeks when I was sleeping fine, the voice and the tracking stuff never went away.\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voice while not feeling especially up or energized?\n\nPatient: Yeah, definitely. Like I was just saying, there was that quieter time, a few weeks there, where I was sleeping a lot more. I wasn't feeling all revved up or staying awake all night making those huge plans for my custom shop. I felt pretty normal, not energized at all. But even then, during those quiet weeks, I still heard the voice out in the garage. And I still knew they were tracking me—my husband and my boss. \n\nIt's weird how they think they can hide it, honestly. Like my boss, he thinks he's so slick, but I know how the shop's Wi-Fi network is set up. We have this router in the back office, right? And it's one of those commercial ones with the big antennas. The guy from the internet company came out to install it, and he had this huge spool of CAT6 cable. He was complaining the whole time because he had to run it through the drop ceiling, and the ceiling tiles in the shop are covered in this thick layer of black dust from the exhaust fumes. Whenever you move a tile, it just rains black soot everywhere. I had to wipe down my entire toolbox afterward. My toolbox is a Snap-on, cherry red. Cost me more than my first car, but it's worth it because the drawers have those soft-close glides. If you slam a drawer full of heavy sockets in a cheap box, the whole thing rattles and eventually the tracks bend. I saw a guy drop a whole drawer of half-inch drive impact sockets on his foot once because the track gave out. Broke three toes. He had to wear this special boot for a month, and he couldn't even press the clutch pedal on his own car... \n\nBut yeah, anyway, even when I wasn't feeling up or energized for those couple of weeks, the voice and the tracking were definitely still there.\n\nDoctor: Before you first started hearing the voice ten months ago, had you ever had a period like this where you needed much less sleep and felt unusually energized?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually. The whole thing with the long stretches of getting barely any sleep, having all these racing plans for the shop, and just nonstop activity... that all started about eleven months ago. So, yeah, a little before the voice showed up. \n\nI remember because that was right around the time I decided I was going to completely rebuild the transmission on this '98 Silverado we had sitting in the back lot. I was up for like three days straight just tearing into it. Transmissions are a totally different beast, you know? A lot of mechanics won't even touch the internals. They just swap the whole unit out and call it a day. It is literally the worst smell on earth. It’s this sharp, metallic, rotten fish smell that just gets into your pores. You can take three showers and you still smell like burnt ATF. My husband actually made me sleep on the couch that week because of the smell. Well, that and because I was pacing around the living room at 3 AM drawing up blueprints for the transmission dyno I was going to build from scratch. I even went out and bought all this steel tubing to weld the frame for it. Welding is tricky though, especially TIG welding. You need a really steady hand, and you have to get the argon gas flow just perfect or the weld gets all porous and weak. I watched this guy on TV build a whole sand rail frame in like two days, but they edit out all the prep work. The prep work is like ninety percent of welding. You have to grind off all the mill scale and clean the joints with acetone, otherwise the puddle just pops and spits at you. But even then, I still heard the voice out in the garage, and I still knew for a fact that my husband and boss were tracking me. \n\nIt's just crazy how they go about it. Like my husband, he's always on his phone, acting like he's just playing games or whatever, but I know he's checking the location app. He's got this old iPhone, the screen is completely shattered in the corner. It's actually not that hard if you have the right tools, but the screws are tiny. Like, microscopic. You have to use this special little pentalobe screwdriver, and if you sneeze, you lose half the screws on the carpet. I had to use a magnet to find one I dropped. Magnets are a lifesaver in the shop, too. We have these long magnetic pickup tools for when you drop a socket down into the engine bay. Because there is nothing worse than dropping a 10-millimeter socket. It's like they just disappear into another dimension. You can shine a flashlight down there for an hour and never find it. I swear there's a black hole at the bottom of every engine bay just for 10-millimeter sockets. The ones with the nice glossy pictures of classic cars, they want like twenty bucks for them at the auto parts store. I usually just wait until February when they put them on clearance for two dollars. Though last year I got this really cool one that had vintage muscle cars, and January was a '69 Chevelle SS. You know, some people try to fake it, they put a boot over the automatic shifter to make it look like a manual, but anyone who knows anything about cars can spot that from a mile away. It's one of those rugged ones, encased in rubber so if you drop it on the concrete floor of the shop, it doesn't shatter. Concrete is unforgiving. I dropped a brand new torque wrench on the floor once and it completely threw off the calibration. You have to send them out to get recalibrated, and it takes weeks. You can't just guess with torque specs, especially on things like cylinder head bolts. If you over-torque them, you stretch the bolts and ruin the threads in the block. If you under-torque them, you blow a head gasket. It's a very precise science. People think mechanics just hit everything with an impact gun until it's tight, but that's how you snap bolts. You know, we have a lot of cars that come into the shop that haven't had an oil change in ten months, or even a year, and the oil comes out looking like black sludge. People just ignore the sticker on their windshield. They think synthetic oil means they can just drive forever without changing it. But the filter still gets clogged, you know? It doesn't tell you the exact part that failed. You still have to do the actual diagnostic work. It could be a vacuum leak, it could be a clogged fuel injector, it could be a bad mass airflow sensor. I spent three hours last Tuesday smoke-testing the intake on a Chevy Cruze trying to find a leak. Those 1.4-liter Ecotec engines are notorious for PCV issues. People just hear what they want to hear, you know? They think if they ask the question enough times, the answer will magically change to something cheaper or easier. \n\nBut my answer isn't changing.
